facts.fact: ~50 billion pieces of litter on US roadways (23.7B) and waterways (25.9B); 152 per US resident
facts.source: Keep America Beautiful 2020 National Litter Study

facts.fact: Cigarette butts are the single most littered item in the US: 19.6% of all litter
US roadway litter down 54% since 2009 (51.2B -> 23.7B pieces)
Nearly 350 million plastic bags and 394.7 million fast-food cups littered; 90% of residents say litter is a problem in their state

Tulip mania: Alkmaar auction 5 Feb 1637; Haarlem sale failed 3 Feb 1637; collapse by end of first week of Feb; Semper Augustus reportedly f10,000; skilled craftsman ~f300/yr; Goldgar: ~285 Haarlem buyers, almost no bankruptcies, canal suicides 'more fiction than fact'
facts.source: History Today (Goldgar 2007/2018); History.com (Roos); Wikipedia Tulip mania

facts.fact: Most cigarette filters are cellulose acetate (plastic-like); UV breaks one filter into thousands of tiny microplastics; butts = #1 item at the International Coastal Cleanup for 25+ years; 2,412,151 collected worldwide in 2017
facts.source: NOAA Ocean Service 'most common ocean litter' (updated 09/23/26) + NOAA Marine Debris Program blog (2018-09-10)

facts.fact: Leachate from smoked cigarette butts (filter + tobacco): 96-hour LC50 ~1 butt per liter for both topsmelt (marine, 1.1/L) and fathead minnow (freshwater, 0.97/L), i.e. ~1 butt/L killed half the test fish
facts.source: Slaughter E, Gersberg RM, Watanabe K, Rudolph J, Stransky C, Novotny TE. Tobacco Control 2011;20(Suppl 1):i25-i29 (San Diego State University)

facts.fact: NOAA Marine Debris Program: 'We may not know exactly how long it takes for plastic and other materials to break down'; short history of plastics, 'absence of reliable data, and only a few peer-reviewed studies'; plastics 'could stay in the ocean and Great Lakes for an indefinite amount of time'. Popular round numbers (e.g. aluminum can 200 years) have little science behind them (Harold Johnson, Scientific American guest blog 'Time to Can the Round Numbers').
facts.source: NOAA Marine Debris Program blog, 'The Mystery of How Long Until It's Gone' (Sept 1, 2020); Scientific American guest blog

facts.fact: Great Molasses Flood: Jan 15, 1919 ~12:30-1 PM; 50-ft tank, ~2.3M gallons; ~35 mph; wave height reported 15-40 ft (Britannica) / 30 ft (NPR); 21 killed, ~150 injured; knocked an Elevated train off its tracks (Boston.gov); tank leaked, painted brown to hide it (Boston.gov, NPR); owners blamed anarchists; 1925 auditor ruled owners' negligence, damages paid; smell 'for years' (Britannica), folklore on hot days (NPR).
